title: ✨ Planetary Conjunction — Venus & Saturn (0.9° apart)
description:
Venus (magnitude −4.1) and Saturn (magnitude +1.2) appear just 0.9° apart — close enough to fit within a single binocular field of view. Look west 45 minutes after sunset.

Brilliant Venus passes just 0.9° from Saturn in the evening sky, with Saturn appearing as a golden dot just to Venus's lower left. The pair will be visible low in the west for about 45 minutes after sunset — binoculars will reveal Saturn's disk and hint at its rings. Saturn will move into the Sun's glare within days of this conjunction, making this a brief observing window.

title: ✨ Planetary Conjunction — Venus & Jupiter (1.6° apart)
description:
Venus (magnitude −4.5) and Jupiter (magnitude −2.0) appear just 1.6° apart — close enough to fit within a single binocular field of view. Look west-northwest 45 minutes after sunset.

The two brightest planets in the sky — Venus and Jupiter — come within 1.6° of each other, fitting within the field of view of most binoculars. Venus blazes at magnitude −4.5 while Jupiter shines at −2.0. The pair is unmissable in the western sky after sunset, outshining everything except the Moon. This is one of the year's most spectacular naked-eye events.

title: ✨ Planetary Conjunction — Venus & Mercury (2.0° apart)
description:
Venus (magnitude −4.2) and Mercury (magnitude +0.5) appear just 2.0° apart — close enough to fit within a single binocular field of view. Look west just after sunset.

Venus and Mercury appear close together in the evening twilight. Brilliant Venus at magnitude −4.2 acts as a guidepost for spotting elusive Mercury, which is rarely easy to observe. Look low in the west shortly after sunset; binoculars will show both planets in the same field of view against the twilight glow.

title: ✨ Planetary Conjunction — Jupiter & Mars (1.2° apart)
description:
Jupiter (magnitude −2.3) and Mars (magnitude +1.1) appear just 1.2° apart — close enough to fit within a single binocular field of view. Look east before dawn.

Jupiter and Mars converge to within 1.2° of each other in the pre-dawn sky, rising around midnight and climbing high by dawn. The color contrast is striking — Jupiter shines as a brilliant white-yellow beacon while Mars glows distinctly reddish-orange. Both planets fit easily within a binocular field of view, and a small telescope will show Jupiter's cloud bands and four Galilean moons alongside Mars's reddish disk.

title: ✨ Planetary Conjunction — Venus & Jupiter (3.5° apart)
description:
Venus (magnitude −4.0) and Jupiter (magnitude −2.1) appear just 3.5° apart — close enough to fit within a single binocular field of view. Look east before dawn.

Venus and Jupiter appear together in the morning sky, separated by about 3.5°. Both planets rise well before the Sun, making this an easy naked-eye event from a clear eastern horizon. The two brightest planets make a striking pair against the pre-dawn sky.
